title: Why Static Typing Came Back • Richard Feldman • GOTO 2022
summary: Richard Feldman explains why dynamic languages won the early web and why modern static typing removed the ceremony, slow feedback and unhelpful errors that made them lose.

assertions.quote: these benefits don't require Dynamic typing they just first appeared in Dynamic languages

verdicts.note: A plausible historical account consistent with language-adoption timelines, but causal attribution from history is not testable.

assertions.quote: some languages and Community Norms encourage ceremony but they don't have to
all of these things do not have any nil null or undefined errors in production all of them 100 have been caught at build time
this right here is a fast feedback loop seeing this error right there as you're writing your code

verdicts.note: Developer surveys cite this as TypeScript's main benefit; measured productivity gains from type feedback are modest in experiments.

For both type-error fixing tasks Java (compile error) beat Groovy (run-time no-such-method failure) significantly in both groups; mean times 78s vs 149s and 44s vs 246s, so a static error message is faster feedback than running the program and tracing the failure.

All indicators (time, test runs, files opened, file switches) favoured the static type system on type-error tasks because the compiler names the location while a run-time failure appears far from the cause; the feedback came from a compiler in a plain text editor, not an in-editor checker, so the claim's in-editor form is an extrapolation.

assertions.quote: there's no way to get a dynamically typed language to be as fast as the fastest possible statically type language
it has very serious unavoidable downsides that just come with the territory of deciding that you want gradual types

verdicts.note: Type-system complexity in TypeScript and Sorbet supports this, though gradual typing's migration benefit is real.

assertions.quote: when these go from sort of blocking compile errors to non-blocking error reports that are just informative wow this just becomes sort of all upside

verdicts.note: TypeScript's emit-on-error demonstrates feasibility; the productivity claim is anecdotal.
